rows.verified: COSHH requires employers to adequately control exposure to workplace materials that can cause ill health.
Hazardous workplace substances can include dusts, gases, fumes, liquids, gels, powders and harmful microorganisms.
Lead, asbestos and radioactive substances are controlled by separate specific regulations rather than COSHH.
Employers should identify health hazards and assess how workers could be harmed before deciding controls.
Exposure should first be prevented at source by avoiding the hazardous substance, using a safer process or substituting a safer form or product where practicable.
Where prevention is not possible, exposure must be adequately controlled and the risk of harm made as low as reasonably practicable.
COSHH controls can combine enclosure, local exhaust ventilation, procedures, supervision, training, maintenance, PPE and worker behaviour.
Employers should keep controls working, provide information and training, use monitoring or health surveillance where appropriate and plan for emergencies.
COSHH controls depend on the substance, form, concentration, exposure route, task, duration, workforce and effectiveness of existing controls.
COSHH evidence is substance-, process- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Employers should identify which jobs and activities create exposure before specifying a local exhaust ventilation system.
The required performance of LEV should be written down and the correct type selected to control the source effectively.
Workers should be involved in LEV design or selection so the system can be used effectively in real tasks.
LEV should be commissioned before use to confirm adequate control, prove performance and create a benchmark for later examinations.
LEV should have airflow indicators or an equivalent means of showing that it is operating correctly.
Suppliers should provide a user manual and logbook or equivalent records for the installed LEV system.
LEV users need training, routine checks, correct positioning and prompt reporting of smells, settled dust, unusual noise or other faults.
LEV must be maintained in efficient order, thoroughly examined and tested at least every 14 months, with examination records kept for at least five years.
LEV performance depends on the contaminant source, hood design, airflow, process conditions, worker position, maintenance and commissioning data.
LEV evidence is process-, system- and operating-condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level inhalation-risk probability.
